How should conditional probability be interpreted?
options: As chance before any information is known
As the number of outcomes in the sample space
As the complement of ordinary probability
As chance after learning that the condition has occurred

questions.question: If $P(A\cap B)=0.2$ and $P(B)=0.5$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
A die roll is known to be even. What is the probability it is six?
Which is a conditional probability question?
options: The number of possible laptops in a store, for every possible choice of input.
The probability of the whole sample space
The probability a customer buys a warranty given they bought a laptop

questions.question: If $A\subseteq B$ and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
How does the multiplication rule follow from conditional probability?
options: Replace every conditional probability by a complement
Rearrange $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ to get $P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B)$

questions.question: Why can $P(A\mid B)$ differ from $P(A)$?
options: Learning that $B$ occurred can change the relevant reference cases
Conditional probabilities are always larger than ordinary probabilities

questions.question: Bayes' rule expresses $P(B\mid A)$ using which quantities?
options: $P(A\cap B)$ alone, with no other terms

questions.question: If $P(B)=0.25$ and $P(A\mid B)=0.6$, what is $P(A\cap B)$?
If $A$ and $B$ are independent and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
In a group of $30$ students, $12$ study statistics and $6$ study both statistics and economics. What is the probability of economics given statistics?
Why is $P(A\mid B)$ not generally the same as $P(B\mid A)$?
options: The denominators $P(B)$ and $P(A)$ are generally different
The two expressions always use the same denominator
Conditional probability is symmetric by definition

questions.question: If $P(A\mid B)=1$ with $P(B)>0$, which interpretation is correct?
options: $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, so observing $B$ rules out $A$.
$P(A)$ must be zero before conditioning on $B$.
Among outcomes where $B$ occurs, $A$ occurs with probability one.
